clue.text: Dead embarrassed accepting hand heartless lady granted

indicators.note: accepting means the jumbled letters take in the next piece
embarrassed suggests being thrown into confusion, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

parts.note: a mitt is slang for a hand

indicators.note: heartless means the middle of the word lady is cut out, leaving its outside letters

explanation.surface: A mortified man is made to accept the hand of a cold-hearted woman, his wish granted after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead embarrassed' reads as utterly mortified, but 'embarrassed' is the anagram signal working on Dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are concessive adverbs: 'granted, it was late' and 'admittedly, it was late' concede a point the same way.

clue.text: Tea with last slice of lemon in that's only just been made?

indicators.note: in means these pieces go inside the tea

parts.note: a brew is a pot or cup of tea
and means together with

indicators.note: last slice of picks the final letter of the word lemon

explanation.surface: A cup of tea with a final sliver of lemon dropped in, freshly made.
explanation.definitionFit: Something freshly manufactured, never used, is described as fresh off the production line; the phrase describes exactly that recency.

clue.text: Destroy decrepit touring vehicle — use this to get round instead

definitions.text: use this to get round instead

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the jumbled letters travel around the vehicle
decrepit means broken down, so the letters of the word Destroy are worn into a new order

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: An instruction to scrap a clapped-out touring car and travel some other way.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram letters go round the vehicle, which sits before their final letter. The answer is the smart card used to pay fares on London's buses and Tube.
explanation.definitionFit: The travel smartcard is what Londoners tap to get around by public transport rather than by car.

clue.text: Charge round interrupting 19

indicators.note: interrupting means the round letter breaks into the middle of the other word

parts.note: the answer to 19 across is a young person, a lad
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A charge is laid while someone is interrupted; mostly a cross-reference with little picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Charge and load are synonyms for what a gun or battery is filled with, or what is put in it.

clue.text: Mind training for novice in top celebrity run

indicators.note: for means one thing stands in place of another

parts.note: an A-lister is a celebrity on the top list
L is a learner, from the learner plate
training means putting the word Mind through a reshaping, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mental training for a beginner within a run led by a top celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' turns MIND into DMIN, which replaces the L in A-LISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To run an organisation or a process is to manage it, which is what administering means.

clue.text: Sweet-talk model believing head's gone

indicators.note: model as a verb means shape, so the remaining letters are fashioned into a new order
head's gone means the first letter of believing is dropped

explanation.surface: Charming a model into believing something once her senses have gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to win someone over with flattery and coaxing.

clue.text: Ray adopts Republican slogan

indicators.note: adopts means the fish takes in the letter

parts.note: a manta is a large species of ray fish

explanation.surface: A man named Ray takes up a Republican catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a man's name; it is the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase repeated over and over, as a political slogan is, is loosely called a mantra.

clue.text: See 3
Why on earth argue about old money? It may offend

indicators.note: on means the letter comes after the earth

parts.note: dirt is soil, earth
the letter Y is named exactly like the word why

indicators.note: about means the word for argue is turned round

parts.note: to row is to argue
d was the abbreviation for a penny in old British money

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'why on earth' at arguing over obsolete currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Why on earth' reads as an exclamation, but it splits into the letter Y placed after earth. Before decimalisation in 1971, British pennies were written d.
explanation.definitionFit: A word that people find offensive, or a topic considered taboo, is called by this phrase.

clue.text: Half of sisters like girl's name

indicators.note: half of means the first two letters of the four-letter word for sisters

parts.note: nuns are sisters of a religious order
a la means in the manner of, like

explanation.surface: Half of a group of sisters share a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an Irish girl's first name, so it fits the definition directly.

clue.text: Light in the past — dieting worked

indicators.note: worked means kneaded or reshaped, so the letters of dieting are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone once light, because their diet worked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like slim; it is the verb, and 'in the past' puts it into the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Lit and set fire to are past forms of the verb to light, as is the word sought.

clue.text: Fancied fish — considered not having starter

parts.note: the ide is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: not having starter means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: rated means considered, judged

explanation.surface: Someone fancied a fish but thought better of a starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancied' looks like desired; it means imagined.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy in the sense of imagine or conceive is to form an idea of something.

clue.text: Drift to one side round middle of bend

indicators.note: round means the first pieces surround the next
middle of picks the central letters of the word bend

parts.note: R is right, one side

explanation.surface: A car drifting to one side as it rounds the middle of a bend.
explanation.definitionFit: The general drift of an argument is its purport or gist, also called its tenor.

clue.text: Get outta here! One doesn't appreciate what it costs

parts.note: go is a command to leave
an ingrate is an ungrateful person

explanation.surface: A dismissive shout at someone ungrateful, followed by talk of the price.
explanation.definitionFit: The usual market price for something, the standard charge, is described by this phrase.

clue.text: Enters carrying food, so don't hold back!

indicators.note: carrying means the first piece holds the second

parts.note: gets in means enters
tuck is British slang for food, especially snacks

explanation.surface: Someone comes in with food, so the cry is to dig in.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an urging to begin eagerly and with full effort, as diners are urged to eat.

clue.text: Stormy on end of line — where is the president?

indicators.note: stormy means turbulent, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.words: on end of line — where is
parts.note: the letters of on, the end of line (E) and where is, as fodder

explanation.surface: On a stormy telephone line, someone asks where the president is.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwight D. Eisenhower was the 34th President of the United States.

clue.text: Cool in a minor way?

parts.note: the phrase means fashionable among the young; read literally, minors are kids, and being down with them is being cool in a minor way

explanation.walkthrough: 'minor' looks like slight; it means children.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone keeping up with youth culture, trendy as young people see it.

clue.text: This will cater for the rest of the passengers

definitions.text: This will cater for the rest of the passengers

parts.words: This will cater for the rest of the passengers
parts.note: rest means sleep, not the remaining passengers: a railway sleeping car caters for their repose

explanation.walkthrough: 'the rest of the passengers' reads as the others; it is their sleep. It is the French term for a sleeping car on a continental train.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeping carriage on European trains provides berths where travellers sleep overnight.

clue.text: Hinted setter's bed contains a lot of bugs

parts.note: the setter is I, so setter's is I'm, I am

indicators.note: contains means the bed holds what follows

parts.note: pit is slang for bed

indicators.note: a lot of means most, but not all, of the word for bugs, its last letter dropped

parts.note: lice are bugs

explanation.surface: The setter complains that his bed is crawling with bugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implied but not said outright is hinted at, which is how this adjective is used.

clue.text: Solver gets extremely near solution for one of the above

parts.note: the solver is addressed as you

indicators.note: solution means dissolving, so the letters are broken up and remixed
extremely picks the outer letters of near

explanation.surface: The solver nearly reaches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A kid is a young person, one of the minors in the clue above.

clue.text: "21 down", son says

parts.note: the answer to 21 down means complete, also utter

explanation.surface: A son is quoted saying something; mostly a cross-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaks and voices are synonyms of this verb, which means pronounces words.

clue.text: Snap elastic getting in close for knee trembler

indicators.note: getting in means the next letter goes inside
elastic means stretchy and pliable, so the letters of Snap are reshaped
close for picks the final letter of knee

explanation.surface: Elastic snapping causes a knee trembler, a quick hurried encounter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elastic' makes ASPN from SNAP; a 'knee trembler' is British slang for a hasty standing tryst, but 'knee' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The quaking aspen is a tree whose leaves flutter in the slightest breeze, so it trembles.

clue.text: Consummate one relationship in the van — angry words follow

parts.note: A is one

indicators.note: in the van means at the front, so the first letter of relationship

parts.note: a rant is an angry speech

explanation.surface: Consummating a relationship in the back of a van, then a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consummate' looks like a verb; it is the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: As adjectives both mean complete, utter, out-and-out, as in an arrant fool.

clue.text: So defending what the Sun produces is wicked?

indicators.note: defending means surrounding and protecting what follows

parts.note: sic means thus, so
a tan is produced by the sun

explanation.surface: Is the Sun newspaper's output really wicked?
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Sun' looks like the British tabloid; it is the star.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish and evil are synonyms; this one literally refers to Satan.

clue.text: Held up in Gatwick — customs are disgusting

indicators.note: Held up says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone held up in Gatwick customs complains it is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'Held up' reads upwards. Gatwick is a London airport.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal speech, things that are terrible or awful are said to suck.

clue.text: Sticker, it's on old dish

parts.note: a burr is a prickly seed head that sticks
it, with 's meaning is

explanation.surface: Something sticky has landed on an old plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Mexican filled tortillas are a dish, an example of the definition.

clue.text: Following story about strike

indicators.note: about means the word for story is turned round

parts.note: a fib is a story, a lie

explanation.surface: A news story following a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A biff is a blow; to biff is to strike someone.

clue.text: My Joe's best friend?

parts.note: cor is an exclamation of surprise, like my!
a GI Joe is an American soldier, GI

explanation.surface: Someone asks if their Joe is their best friend.
explanation.walkthrough: A dog is man's best friend; this breed was favoured by Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog is called man's best friend, and this Welsh breed is one example.

clue.text: Very silly wearing hat to keep cool

parts.note: in clothes means wearing them
to fan is to cool
tile is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: It is very silly to wear a hat to keep cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to keep' is link; 'wearing' and 'cool' look surface but give the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Childish behaviour is very silly, which is the sense of the adjective.
